sort_cards.title: An arrest
sort_cards.body: Rosa Parks was arrested after refusing to give up her bus seat. Organisers called for people to stay off buses on 5 December. This event helped set off the boycott.
sort_cards.why: The arrest helped prompt the call to act. Unfair rules and earlier action already existed.

sort_cards.title: A change to bus seating
sort_cards.body: After the court order reached Montgomery, the boycott ended on 20 December. People returned to buses on 21 December with the old seating rule removed. The legal case helped secure this change.
sort_cards.why: This is a result by the end of the campaign. It did not end racism or every unfair rule.

sort_cards.title: Unfair bus rules
sort_cards.body: Black passengers faced racist seating rules and unfair treatment on Montgomery buses. These problems had lasted for years. They gave people reasons to seek change.
sort_cards.why: A lasting grievance explains why change was wanted; it was not a new event on 1 December.

sort_cards.title: Links that lasted
sort_cards.date: After the boycott, in later years
sort_cards.body: The campaign built links among people and groups working for civil rights. Those links helped support joint work beyond Montgomery in the years that followed.
sort_cards.why: The focus is continuing links and wider work, not just a new group’s founding date.

sort_cards.title: New ways to travel
sort_cards.body: Many people walked or shared car rides instead of using buses. Volunteers arranged lifts and raised funds. Staying off buses changed daily travel. Shared help also made it easier to keep the protest going.
sort_cards.why: Travel changed during the campaign. It also helped sustain it: an effect can feed back into the protest.

sort_cards.title: Earlier calls for change
sort_cards.body: The Women’s Political Council asked for fairer bus treatment before 1955. It made requests in 1954. Little changed. These problems gave people a reason to seek stronger action.
sort_cards.why: Unresolved grievances form part of the background. The group’s existing links also helped organise action.

sort_cards.title: A model for later protests
sort_cards.date: After the boycott, in later years
sort_cards.body: The boycott showed how people could keep a joint protest going without using violence. Later rights campaigns could draw on that example. It was one influence among many.
sort_cards.why: This concerns influence beyond the campaign. Do not claim it alone caused every later rights change.

sort_cards.title: Fewer bus fares
sort_cards.body: When many passengers stopped using buses, the bus company took in less fare money. This put pressure on the company. It did not, by itself, change the law.
sort_cards.why: Lost fares were an effect during the protest and a source of pressure, not a legal judgement.

legal_process_note.title: A legal case alongside the protest
legal_process_note.body: Four Black women continued the court case Browder v. Gayle. Federal judges ruled against bus segregation on 5 June. The US Supreme Court upheld the ruling on 13 November. The order reached Montgomery in December.
legal_process_note.note: P1 is not a ninth sort card. Link this legal process to card B. Refusing bus travel did not itself overturn the law.

context: In Montgomery, Alabama, USA, racist bus rules kept Black and White riders apart. Black residents and local groups had challenged unfair treatment for years. Rosa Parks was arrested on 1 December 1955. The boycott began on 5 December. Protest, shared work and a legal case all mattered.

model: Unfair bus rules had lasted for years (C), so people wanted change. Parks’s arrest on 1 December 1955 helped trigger the boycott (A). Many people then walked or shared rides (E) because they chose not to use buses. Shared help also kept the protest going. This explains a link, rather than just listing dates.

hinge.question: Which is the trigger for this boycott? A: Unfair rules had lasted for years. B: Parks was arrested on 1 December 1955, prompting a call to act. C: Later campaigns drew on the boycott’s example.
hinge.answer_and_decision_rule: B. A is a long-term cause; C is a later consequence. Ask each pupil privately for a reason. If needed, model before / set off / followed, then use the parallel check before independent work.
hinge.parallel: The bus company took in less fare money during the boycott. Is this a cause that built up before it, or a consequence of staying off buses? It is a short-term consequence. Explain the link: fewer passengers paid fares, so income fell.

staff_care_rules: Teach racism factually and calmly. No copied slurs, discriminatory seating, victim simulation, role play or personal disclosure. Do not ask pupils to defend racist rules or imagine being a targeted person. Historical names and dates are allowed; no living private identities or local school details are used.

Agree the quiet signal, usual supervising adult, safe place and return check before starting. Keep all pupils supervised. If the sole adult cannot safely supervise separate spaces, pause the group or offer a calm area in the room while using the normal support route.

Acknowledge distress without probing. Stop the demand and offer the agreed pause without sanction or a public explanation. Follow existing safeguarding arrangements for disclosures. Do not require a catch-up discussion while a pupil is upset.

Stop racist or flippant remarks calmly and firmly, name the harm without repeating a slur, correct the fact and reset respectful language. Check those affected and follow up privately. Use school procedures for repeated, targeted or serious incidents; do not stage a debate about whether racism is valid.
Offer the neutral task and a private check when ready. Record deferred work as not yet evidenced. A pause task or partner’s answer does not establish the history outcome.

Part
What to know
Long-term causes
Unfair bus rules; earlier requests brought little change.
Trigger

Meaning
cause
A reason why something happened.
long-term cause
A problem or condition that built up over time.
trigger
An event that helps set off action.
consequence
An effect or result of an event or action.
short term
During or near the time of the campaign.
long term
Continuing into later years.
boycott
Not using or buying something as a protest.
segregation
Rules that keep groups apart unfairly.
legal case
An issue taken to a court for a decision.
link
An explanation of how one thing affected another.
limit
What a change did not achieve.
